title: A contact path for a two-sided marketplace
excerpt: Tell the scarce side what happens after they reach out, how fast you reply, and what to have ready. The action is to join. A ten-field form loses them.
alt: A clothing shop with racks, rope-hung industrial lamps, and a mirror, a specific room rather than a generic contact form.
caption: Racks, industrial lamps, and a mirror inside a clothing shop. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a marketplace contact page say above the form?
faqs.answer: Say what happens next, who reads the note, and the reply window you can keep. List what the scarce side should have ready, and state any rule that will get an application refused. A headline about starting a conversation does not answer those questions.

faqs.question: How many fields should the first marketplace form have?
faqs.answer: Four or five is enough for a first yes or no: name, a way to reach them, the city or category, and one sentence on what they offer. Ask for payout details, long biographies, and marketing questions after you have replied. A ten-field form on a phone is a survey, and the careful applicant leaves.

faqs.question: Should hosts and customers share one contact form?
faqs.answer: Give each job its own path, even if one person reads the inbox. An application, a booking question, and a problem with an existing job are different notes. Label them with the same words as the navigation, and publish a reply window for each. One textarea treats the scarce side's application as a generic ticket.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
The two-sided marketplace contact page should tell the side you need first what happens after they reach out, how fast, and what to have ready. The action is to join that side. A form with ten fields is a way to lose them before you have earned a reply.

This page is not a general inbox for the whole internet. It is the last step of a decision that started with a match. If it feels like a new beginning, with a blank "How can we help?", you have thrown away the context they already gave you.

## Say what happens next

Write the sequence above the form, in three lines. You send the form. A named role reads it. You reply with a yes, a no, or one question. If there is a review, say what the review checks. If the founder reads every application this month, say the founder.

The sequence should match the promise on the about page and the services page. A contact path that says "we will be in touch" while the about page names a two-day review is two companies. Pick the true sequence and use it in both places.

Tell them what a yes looks like. An account they can finish. A call of a stated length. A listing that goes up only after a menu is confirmed. Vague acceptance is how people assume they are live when they are not, then tell a friend the market is broken.

Also say what silence means. If no reply within the stated window means they should write again, say that, and say where. A form that vanishes into a queue with no rule trains people to submit twice or to give up. Both are expensive.

## Say how fast, and mean it

Publish a window you can keep on a bad week. Two business days. Same day if the note arrives before noon in a named time zone. "As soon as possible" is not a window. It is a hope, and the scarce side has heard it from markets that never wrote back.

If the window slips, change the sentence before you change the story you tell yourself. A page that still says "within a day" while the inbox is at five days is a false ad sitting on the most trust-sensitive screen you have. Update the page. Then clear the queue.

Speed is also the speed of the page itself. A contact screen that waits on a heavy script before the form can be typed will lose the person who opened it in a break between jobs. The form should be usable when the HTML arrives. Enhancement can wait.

Nielsen Norman Group's research is a reminder that the visit is already short. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds when the value is unclear. A contact page whose first screen is a stock photo and a headline about "starting a conversation" spends that time on nothing they can use. Lead with the window and the list of what to have ready.

## What they should have ready

Put the list before the fields, so the form does not feel like a pop quiz.

For a host: city, kitchen address, a sample menu, the nights they can actually cook. For a carrier: lanes, equipment, a way to receive a rate. For a clinician: license state, the kind of visit, the hours they will take. Ask only for what the next human needs in order to say yes or no.

Leave the rest for after the reply. Bank details, insurance uploads, a long biography, and a taxonomy of "goals" can wait until you have told them they are in. Asking for a payout account from someone you may refuse is a good way to collect data you do not need and to scare the person you did want.

Say which items are required for a first look and which can be rough. "A menu can be a photo of a page. It does not need to be designed." That sentence raises the number of real applications more reliably than a longer brand essay. People delay because they think you want a performance.

If some applicants will be refused on a rule, state the rule here. City, credential, capacity. A person outside the rule can stop, which is kinder than a form that pretends everyone is welcome and a template rejection three days later.

## A short form

Four or five fields is enough for the first reply. Name. A way to reach them. The city, lane, or category. One sentence on what they offer. A checkbox that they read the refusal rule, if you have one.

Ten fields, with dropdowns for company size, budget, timeline, "how did you hear about us," and a message box under a label that says "Tell us about yourself," is a survey. The scarce side did not come to be surveyed. They came to join a market. Each extra field is a place to abandon the page, and on a phone it is a place to abandon it with one thumb.

The W3C WCAG principles ask for content to be understandable: labels, instructions, and a way to know what went wrong. Every field needs a visible label, not only a placeholder that disappears when they type. If they miss a field, say which one, in text, next to the field. A red outline with no words fails that principle and fails ordinary patience.

Do not ask them to pick a side again if the path they followed already picked it. A host who tapped "Apply as a host" should see a host form. A hidden field can carry the side. A second question that says "I am a..." tells them the previous page was not listening.

## Two sides, two paths

The other side may need a contact path of its own. A diner with a refund question should not land in the host application, and a host should not land in a general support box that treats them as a ticket. Split the paths by job: apply, book, and a problem with an existing job.

Label them with the same words as the navigation. "Apply as a host." "Help with a booking." "Something went wrong on a load." A single "Contact us" page with one textarea forces every type of note into one pile, and the scarce side's application sits under a password reset.

If you are small and one person reads all of it, you can still show three labels. They can arrive in one inbox with a subject line that names the job. The page does not have to pretend you have three departments. It has to stop pretending every note is the same note.

Put the response window on each path, because the windows may differ. Applications in two business days. Safety issues the same day. Press and partnerships whenever you can. Do not let a partnership form outrank the application in visual weight. The side you are seeding is the reason the page exists.

## Confirmation that does not vanish

After they submit, the page should repeat what happens next and the window, and it should offer a copy by email if you can send one without a new marketing subscription bundled in. The confirmation is part of the promise. A blank "Thanks!" with a link back home makes people unsure the form worked, so they send it again.

Say whether they should create an account now or wait. If the account exists only after approval, do not send them into a signup that will fail. If they can save a draft, say how to return. A magic link beats a password they invent in a hurry and then lose.

Give them one human address only if a person reads it. A published address that bounces, or that feeds a void, is worse than no address. If the plan for the company is a form and not a mailbox, commit to the form and the window. Do not print an email "for a personal touch" that nobody owns.

Keep a record of what the page promised on the day they applied. When you tighten a rule, people already in the queue are still under the old sentence. Honor it or write to them. The contact path is an operation, not a component you restyle when the brand updates.

## Review the path the way the inbox will feel it

Submit the form yourself on a phone, then wait the window you published. Read the confirmation as if you were nervous about a truck, a kitchen, or a license. If you cannot tell whether you are in a queue, you will not be calmer than your applicants.

Open the note that arrived. Check that the side, the city, and the one sentence are visible without a scavenger hunt through metadata. If the reviewer has to open five systems to understand a four-field form, the path is still too clever. Simplify the note before you add a field.

Once a month, compare the page's window with the actual replies. If the gap is more than a day, fix the operation or fix the sentence. Leaving the sentence because it "sounds better" is how a contact page becomes fiction.

A clean path still fails if the rest of the site performs taste instead of a match. The cuts are in [what not to put on the site for a two-sided marketplace](/blog/what-not-to-put-on-the-site-for-a-two-sided-marketplace).

If you want to look at the path as an operation, not only as a form component, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min).
